title: GraphQL Basics for Frontend Developers

subtopics.title: Schema
subtopics.explanation: A GraphQL server publishes a schema: the types of data and actions a client can ask for. It is like a menu that lists what a kitchen can prepare. The schema gives client and server teams a shared contract.

subtopics.title: Query
subtopics.explanation: A query names the fields the client needs. A page can ask for a product name and price without requesting every field. This can reduce over-fetching, but the server still needs limits for expensive queries.

subtopics.title: Resolver
subtopics.explanation: A resolver is server code that finds the value for one field. It may read a database or call another service. Resolver design affects speed and prevents a page request from triggering too many hidden calls.

subtopics.title: Mutation
subtopics.explanation: A mutation asks the server to change data. It should validate input, check permission, and return enough information for the UI to update. Treat a mutation like submitting a signed form, not a local state change.

subtopics.title: Frontend use
subtopics.explanation: A frontend client sends a query and receives a result shaped around requested fields. Handle loading and errors, and avoid treating the schema as permission to read every record.

foundations.overview: GraphQL lets a client describe which fields it wants from an API.
foundations.whyItMatters: These ideas affect how quickly, reliably, and safely a frontend works.
foundations.browserPerspective: The browser usually sends GraphQL over HTTP, while the server validates and resolves each query.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Use it when clients benefit from selecting fields or combining related data.
foundations.businessImpact: A shared schema can speed product work, but complex resolvers need monitoring.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Keep authorization in server resolvers and make query ownership clear.
foundations.performanceImpact: Set query depth or cost limits and watch for repeated resolver calls.

commonMisconceptions.reality: A query can be expensive; measure resolver work and returned data.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A field in the schema is safe for every user
commonMisconceptions.reality: The server still must check what each user may access.
